An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.106 (statistical) ± 0.014 (systematic) ± 0.006 (model-based).

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs. It establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method.

Our investigation focuses on cosmic-ray anisotropies at high energies exceeding 4 EeV, utilizing data collected by the Pierre Auger Observatory from 2004 to 2016. By employing the maximum-likelihood method, we analyzed the right ascension distribution of 1.44 million high-energy cosmic rays, and found that their anisotropy pattern shifts with galactic coordinates, primarily influenced by the Milky Way's gas clouds. Contrary to previous studies based on smaller data sets, we found no evidence to support a dipole model that accounts for the anisotropy when observing in the galactic plane, and instead, we determined constraints on possible plane-based and intrinsic sources. However, our results are also consistent with a dipole model defined by plasma components within the Local Supercluster.
This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable.

Measurements of the second Fourier coefficient, v2, fluctuations in particle production have been investigated for lead-lead collisions at a LHC's top energy of 5.02 TeV. Researchers analyzed 10,000 events and studied how v2 fluctuates as a function of transverse momentum and centrality for 12 different collision centralities. Furthermore, correlations between geometric and hydrodynamic factors influencing v2 fluctuations have been explored.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches, we consider inconsistencies that arise from various interpretations of such relationships, including those between columns, between a column and external factors, and between a column and non-determined columns. To effectively handle these inconsistencies, we propose a framework built upon a new concept called tuple repairs, which represent valid alternatives to inconsistent records. We further define properties like a partial order and comparable status for repairs, and explore the challenge of identifying the minimal set of changes necessary to resolve all relationships' inconsistencies. To do this, we reframe the problem as finding a shortest path in a directed graph and offer an exact solution, as well as a heuristic method for large-scale instances. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of our approach through a case study and a comprehensive comparison with existing solutions, including those based on probabilistic modeling and constraint satisfaction.

This study introduces four novel dynamic polynomial-based non-Gaussian exponential family autoregressive models: PPAR, PVAR, PPAR(L), and PVAR(L). These models incorporate flexible, nonlinear, and non-Gaussian frameworks. They leverage polynomial link functions to accommodate diverse regression settings and incorporate time-varying regression parameters to enable flexible modeling of dynamic behavior. Notably, PVAR and PVAR(l) are the first of their kind to provide dynamic negative binomial and Poisson autoregressive frameworks. Furthermore, we develop the KAM estimator for PVAR and PVAR(L) with consistent and asymptotic properties proven for these models. To complement theoretical findings, a Monte Carlo simulation is conducted to evaluate the KAM estimator's performance. Additionally, we apply PVAR to the US unemployment rate, demonstrating its capacity to capture complex dynamics and non-linear behavior. PVAR and its variants offer versatile frameworks for modeling and forecasting non-Gaussian time series with intricate behavior.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDF), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and their corresponding velocities in 3D space, using
descriptor vectors. NDF enables a robot to understand object locations from past
observations, even when the object is moving. We further represent NDF in a way
that accounts for the object's transformations in space, providing a robust
tool for manipulation tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of using
position-based NDF to solve tasks like picking and pushing objects, and show
that pre-trained models can generalize to new objects, distances, and moving
objects from different directions. Our code is available for download.

Using the functional renormalization group, we have updated the universal ratio that describes the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity in ratio $R_{\rho}=\frac{R_{\rm c}}{U}$ from the O(N) universality classes. Specific updates to R from previous calculations are given for the O(4) and O(6) classes, with R values of 2.206(6) and 2.004(5) respectively. New precise estimates for R in the O(1), O(2), O(3), O(5), and O(8) classes are also provided using calculations at the 5-loop order and 3-loop order for the $\epsilon$-expansion. Bypassing the need for fixed point universality, a method is demonstrated to derive R values applicable to lattice models, thus placing bounds R should fall within. R values for the Parisi-Leggett-Wilson model are calculated for R of 1.998(25), 2.021(25), 2.100(100), 2.002(100), 2.011(100), and 2.052(300) for O(1), O(2), O(3), O(5), O(8) classes respectively.

In statistics and machine learning, it is often useful to convert non-convex optimization problems, which can have numerous local minima, into "essentially convex" problems, largely convex with some complex corrections. This transformation is key to understanding the "state evolution" algorithm developed by Doucet and others, which addresses the localized Belief Propagation issue. Building on this foundation, our research provides a fresh, non-rigorous examination of the local Belief Propagation's "essentially convex" landscape by utilizing the Sudakov-Fernique lemma to compare integral operators. This approach also enables us to verify the uniqueness and unique characteristics of the TAP states, as well as develop a corresponding algorithm to identify the relevant state(s). This result can be directly applied to a specific class of problems, including those involving binary variables and a particular type of interaction matrix, by demonstrating that the state evolution analysis yields a unique, locally convex TAP free energy, up to an exponential correction term. This in turn implies that the local minimization of the TAP free energy through state evolution is an effective strategy for a wide range of statistical inference problems, as demonstrated by the success of the third-order local Belief Propagation state evolution in resolving the 2-SAT problem.

While using photometry from stars to measure the atmosphere has primarily been applied to detect air pollution and aerosols, recent research suggests this technique can also quantify the atmospheric contents of exoplanetary systems. This presentation will focus on presenting advancements in the aerosol modeling used in such analysis, detailing the development of retrieval models that combine aerosol properties with photometric observations. These models will be discussed, along with comparisons to other analysis methods and explorations of potential applications in the Solar System, with an emphasis on exploring Saturn's upper atmosphere.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using convolutional neural networks has gained significant interest. Current methods often focus on either regression or matching techniques, neglecting the object's semantic properties. However, in real-world scenarios, objects possess diverse attributes that can influence the accuracy of pose estimation. To address this, we introduce a novel framework combining projection group regression and correspondence learning, called Deep Hierarchical Multi-attribute Projection correspondence correspondence Pose estimation (DeepHMap++). In this framework, we first employ a multi-attribute regression module to identify the pose's semantic group through multiple projected heatmaps. Subsequently, a correspondence learning module refines the position of each pixel's response by analyzing the relationships between the objects' parts. Experiments conducted on the LINEMODE and NASA datasets show that our model outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of accuracy.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix given a set of positive
definite matrix inputs. GGLasso specifically handles both standard and stochastic
scenarios, incorporating a time series construction method with a Kolednik &
Czado (2019) objective function. The package includes a step-wise scribing
algorithm, the ability to manage large-scale datasets, and a variety of
visualization tools for a standard and stochastic examples.

Numerous numerical methods are used to solve molecular dynamics equations, which are essential for understanding the physical and chemical properties of molecules. These properties are closely tied to the arrangement of atoms within the molecule, and their positions are typically determined by statistical models that account for various possible molecular configurations. Unfortunately, these models are difficult to work with due to the complex relationships between different configurations, hindering efficient sampling of the most influential configurations. This sampling difficulty is especially pronounced in large molecules, such as those found in protein folding and long-chain polymer systems. This study presents a novel approach to improving the efficiency of calculating molecular properties by developing a method to accelerate sample generation through modifications to the Langevin Dynamics simulation's configurational sampling step, utilizing an adaptive mesh size that varies across space and configurations, and presenting results that demonstrate significant improvements in sampling efficiency and accuracy, including a suggested range for mesh refinement levels.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations for each layer that can be solved independently.

Recently, we formulated the Schr\"odinger equation in $R$-Minkowski spacetime. In this work, we extend this achievement by deriving the corresponding Dirac equation within the same spacetime framework. A key challenge arises due to the absence of a covariant Schr\"odinger-like equation for a spinor $\Psi$. However, we successfully overcome this obstacle and obtain the desired result.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon entry, specifically in intermediate speed regimes where a key feature known as the surface seal can occur. I have analyzed spheres entering the water surface headfirst at various speeds and impacts points, and observed that air trapped between the sphere and water surface can either be held in place or broken, depending on the speed and impact point. I found that spheres experiencing surface seals experience less water splashing and smaller amounts of air being pushed out of the sphere, which is consistent with existing theories and measurements. However, spheres that have been side-swiped and experienced surface seals exhibit an unusual combination of characteristics, which is not seen in other impacts. Furthermore, I found that an empirical formula can be used to predict when surface seals will occur, and that the spheres' ability to hold onto the surface air increases as their speed does. These findings are relevant to a wide range of situations where water gets trapped inside spheres, including in sports like polo and water polo, as well as in military applications like torpedoes and missiles.

A well-known conjecture posits that for N=2 global or local supersymmetric Einstein-Maxwell theories in four dimensions, all possible consistent generalized theta-terms within their low-energy effective field theories lead to breakage of their electric-magnetic duality symmetries and, as a result, have no all-loop corrections beyond one-loop level, thereby becoming either precisely quantized unphysical values or 0. Our research, however, demonstrates that under an extension of the base theory to N=8 global supersymmetry, all possible consistent generalized theta-terms demand the Yang-Mills fields to be strictly massless, thus explaining the origin of S-duality breaking, quantization, and the source of the "mystery" of why N=2 supersymmetry lacks quartic scalar couplings, which correspond to positive-definite operators. Furthermore, we establish that all possible consistent generalized theta-terms demand the axion-dilaton fields to be frozen at extremely small values of the cosmological constant, which, in turn, necessitates the absence of radiation in the far field region, which, as a result, is not realizable in the context of radiative classical gravity, and, as a further consequence, all possible consistent generalized theta-terms are proven to be precisely quantized unphysical values or 0 in the absence of radiative classical gravity.

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds and is found to be a primary cause of the material's strong electron-phonon coupling.

A significant number of researchers are focusing on the field of solid-state quantum photonics as it allows for efficient generation, manipulation and detection of entangled photon pairs. The process of recombination in MoS2 monolayers results in a lack of spin-orbit coupling and therefore produces intrinsically entangled photon pairs. The researchers in the study successfully measured the maximum amplitude of Rabi oscillations in MoS2 monolayers and found that the Rabi frequency could be modified by adjusting the laser power and wavelength, and even controlled with an internal magnetic field. The study also controlled the dark exciton fraction and found it to be 99%. The researchers also conducted a thought experiment in which they controlled the dark and bright exciton populations and demonstrated that the Rabi oscillations could be fully resolved in the wavelength spectrum of the generated photon pairs. The findings of the study provide a deeper understanding of MoS2 monolayers and their potential applications in the generation of massive entanglement.

Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice belonging to non-symmorphic wallpaper group p2m2, and we analyze its symmetries, space group elements, and associated momentum space features, including high-symmetry lines, points, and lines marked with their respective weights. Using a tight-binding model, we demonstrate the presence of natural Dirac cones at specific K and K' points. By applying periodic modulation, we show how to induce additional, artificial Dirac cones within certain regions of the lattice. Notably, we find that these cones can be eliminated or relocated by adjusting various parameters, and they always reside at the intersection of multiple high-symmetry points. This interaction often results in a complex arrangement of multiple, interlaced lines marking the intersection of certain symmetries.

Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using an empty beam with photons and a intense laser beam, interacted with a non-linear crystal and a mirror, and a special property of quantum catalysis that enables the transfer of a single photon to one of the ports of a beam splitter of any size.
Empirical and graphical methods for detecting and distinguishing SPCCSs from the vacuum state and other competing states are also presented, and it has been shown that a simple parity measurement is an optimal strategy for this purpose.
Furthermore, the application of SPCCSs in enhancing quantum key distribution protocols is explored, and our study indicates that these states can significantly improve the performance of these protocols by nearly an order of magnitude compared to coherent states with the same average photon number.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism.

A recent framework combining machine learning and linear programming has been proposed for designing proteins with novel functionalities. This method leverages biology to create highly efficient versions of natural proteins, exploiting the modularity of genetic information. A similar principle applies to synthetic polymers, which also consist of a sequence of symbols that can be as diverse as proteins. However, unlike proteins, the synthetic nature of polymer polymers lacks the rigorous testing and optimization standards they underwent in their natural forms. Optimizing the sequences of these polymers is crucial for achieving the desired functionalities, a challenge addressed by our new algorithm, PolyMILP. Unlike previous tools, PolyMILP doesn't require the assumption of a co-functionality constraint, enabling it to tackle a broader range of functional challenges than previously possible. We demonstrated the effectiveness of PolyMILP through optimization challenges involving the creation of a stitch-resistant polymer sequence for a famous yellow rubber shoe and a completely water-resistant polymer sequence for a well-known bathing toy. Additionally, our results include the integration of a secondary model to infer the structural characteristics of both polymers.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans is crucial for diagnosing and treating esophageal diseases, and is particularly important in cases of cancer where the extent of spread beyond the esophagus must be determined. However, this process can be complicated by the frequent lack of clear boundaries in CT scans and the frequent appearance of tissues with similar appearances to tumors, such as air pockets and fluids, which can often be misidentified as tumors. In addition, the frequent variation in anatomy and the presence of partially visible tumors in CT scans further complicates the process. To address these challenges, a novel deep learning model, called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet), is proposed to automatically identify tumors in the esophagus in CT scans. This model combines three sub-networks, including two dense units that capture local and global features, and an attention module that differentiates between the features' importance. This model was tested on two publicly available datasets, and demonstrates superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art deep learning models. The DDAUnet achieved a Dice score of 0.78 in the MICCAI 2017 dataset and 0.66 in the KWAC dataset, outperforming comparable models in terms of segmentation accuracy.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective communication across various situations. This multilingual ability may lead to a phenomenon known as code-switching or inserting foreign words into primary sentences, complicating NLP tasks but also presenting an opportunity to develop more accurate, automated systems. To capture the full potential of multilingual NLP models, it is crucial to address the limitations and constraints of the currently used evaluation metrics and dataset construction methods, which may not accurately represent real-world code-switching patterns. To bridge this gap, researchers should critically examine the existing methodologies, particularly in terms of evaluation metrics, dataset annotation, and construction, and explore more nuanced and realistic representations of code-switching in NLP tasks.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines for description-based evaluations and a clearer understanding of how to create and select appropriate reference descriptions. Furthermore, as outlined in Section 3, I outline several potential research directions to explore.

Tantalum oxide compounds, particularly Ta$_2$O$_5$, have drawn attention as promising dielectric materials with high constants, making them suitable replacements for traditional dielectrics in semiconductors. Unlike Ta$_2$O$_3$ and Ta$_2$O$_4$, ta ta Ta$_2$O$_5$ exhibits a stable crystal structure from an abstract point, which has not been observed due to its dynamic scattering pattern that hinders diffraction analysis. By studying the possible Ta$_2$O$_5$ ground state crystal structures, we found two structures to have the most stability, but neither matched the expected diffraction pattern. In search of a match, we examined possible structures with hexagonal close packing of tantalum atoms, discovering a specific structure, $\beta$-Ta$_2$O$_5$, with an orthorhombic crystal system. This structure closely resembled the anticipated diffraction pattern, and with an calculated dielectric constant of 25.1, it demonstrated suitability as a high-performance dielectric material. Furthermore, we identified its most stable variant, $\beta$'-Ta$_2$O$_5$, with a calculated dielectric constant of 25.4. Both structures exhibit metallic properties. Previous studies have characterized the significance of the "big geographic sort" in determining where online information is shared across different platforms of social media. We extend this analysis by examining the prevalence and ramifications of sorting by location in the context of misinformation circulating among U.S. Reddit users between 2016 and 2020. Our investigation uncovers three key observations. Firstly, sorting content based on geography significantly boosts its share of spreading misinformation in multiple subreddits, with this effect being more pronounced than what has been previously reported in other regions. Our data also reveals that larger U.S. states have Subreddit sizes that are disproportionately smaller than their population would suggest. Moreover, our study reveals that misinformation has a disproportionately higher rate of being spread in states with larger sizes of Subreddits, a finding that may be a consequence of sorting by geography, a phenomenon we refer to as "misogeography." Finally, our analysis shows that the size of a Subreddit has a disproportionately smaller size in urban areas when compared to rural areas, with this disparity being more pronounced in smaller Subreddits, which have a higher likelihood of spreading misinformation in larger states.

Human teachers often provide oral demonstrations to robots during task demonstrations, which can enhance the robots' ability to comprehend and remember what is being taught.  To effectively develop and apply more advanced and efficient learning methods that utilize this abundant oral data, it is crucial to gain a deeper understanding of the linguistic patterns of human instructors.  To acquire such insights, we conducted a large-scale analysis of oral instructions given by three instructors showing a robot how to operate it with the use of GUI-based demonstrations, which were recorded as audio and video.  Our examination of these recordings revealed distinct linguistic patterns associated with specific types of information being conveyed during oral instructions, which can be utilized to efficiently design controlled oral instructions for optimizing advanced learning methods that utilize natural language.  Moreover, we discovered that certain instances of controlled instructions that guided the robot's actions could be applied to categorize information that is crucial for the robot to know before commencing a task.  Furthermore, we found that some crucial controlled instructions that guided the robot's actions during controlled instructions could be utilized to enhance achievements of state-of-the-art models that classify information that is crucial for the robot to know before commencing a task.  Our research also shows that the most abundant and valuable linguistic patterns detected during the examination of recorded oral instructions can be utilized to guide the robot in distinguishing between audio instructions given before, during, or after specific actions being performed. Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this challenge is through the study of conformal field theories, specifically $\phi$-PWA fields in two dimensions. A key insight is that these theories possess primary fields that obey operator product expansions and correspond to conserved currents. By exploiting this property, we are able to derive the equations of motion for the primary fields, also known as the equations of motion for holomorphic currents. Assuming that the time and quantum evolution of complex variables representing the current fields can be modeled, we are able to define a dynamic variable representing field theory complexity. Our analysis reveals a striking connection between this complexity and another measure, $\sigma$, first introduced by Jack and Ruskin in 1984. We further investigate the radiation and black hole phases of $c=0$ conformal field theory, observing that the complexity's rate of change is directly related to the total point-like energy density.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior, and the corresponding implications for our testing framework.

Cross-domain recommendation has been widely studied to address the cold-start problem in new domains. However, an under-explored possibility lies in the multiple new domains and the limited data they individually present. In this context, collaboration among such domains offers a more robust solution than a single domain focusing on its own sparse knowledge. Consequently, a novel problem is proposed called multi-sparse-domain recommendation, and initial exploratory solutions are devised. To effectively solve this proposed challenge, an innovative model called MSDRCP that stands for Multi-Sparse-Domain Recommendation via Aspect-based Preference Learning has been designed. This model's key characteristic is the 'comprehensive aspect preference learning' module, which plays a pivotal role in capturing user preferences across various nuanced dimensions including inter-domain relationships and micro-aspects, as well as the unique and common aspect-specific features that distinguish each domain. At a glance level, such issues can be further explored and more suitable models can be developed to enhance the performance of multi-sparse-domain recommendation systems. Unlike most existing single or two-sense domains models, multi-sparse-domain systems often deal with distinct data characteristics, necessitating unique considerations in model design.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. This range of cones includes well-known examples like the positive semidefinite and exponential cones, as well as lesser-known ones such as the Lorentz, relaxed total nonnegative, and several types of elliptical cones. By utilizing the Hypatia.jl package, we have been able to effectively address these natural conic formulations in their convex optimization solutions. In our performance testing, Iterative Cutting-Plane and Elliptical Packing algorithms delivered outstanding results when working with exotic cones. These performance estimates are expressed in comparison to standard formulations, for which our approach achieves a cutting-edge performance. This approach also takes into consideration the unique properties of certain cones, for instance, a NOP-cone formulation that exhibits 60 percent less computational delay than an equivalent positive semidefinite formulation.

The escalating quantity of human neuroimaging data necessitates automated quality control methods. Our proposed deep learning framework successfully identifies anomalous MRI scans, even with minimal reference data consisting of high-quality images. Our method treats quality control as an outlier detection task and employs a deep autoencoder to reconstruct normal brain images, flagging potential problems when encountering difficult image patterns. Experiments demonstrate the model's effectiveness across various generalization scenarios, including distribution shifts caused by intensity distortions, geometric transformations, image artifacts, and pathological conditions. Notably, our approach also excels in minimizing the reliance on reference data, performing well with both large and small datasets of healthy brain images, and even with normal brain images alone.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids after outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates their dispatch, movement, and self-sufficient driving capabilities. Unlike previous studies, this approach accounts for their flexibility in a more comprehensive manner. However, due to its complexity, solving this model is computationally demanding. To overcome this limitation, we created an efficient multi-agent optimization framework that breaks down the model into manageable parts. Our research also explores various charging strategies and movement patterns to identify flexible periods when power lines are disrupted. Furthermore, we used real-world data from a specific power grid outage to demonstrate and validate our methods, leading to insightful findings about the potential of private electric vehicles to enhance grid resilience during critical periods.

The motivation models that explain how individual agents' social drives influence their actions have gained considerable interest in recent years. To test and improve the social rendezvous strategy of a single agent with others present, our work employs recurrent scenarios where the agent must meet specific targets while competing with distractors. We find that randomly selected target agents are frequently overlooked due to their smaller body size. The recent social rendezvous model shows recurring trials successfully meet the target agent in the majority of cases. The model also exhibits proactive planning behavior similar to that of five-year-old children in a comparable scenario.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and a series of GdxCm1-xSn3 compounds with varying compositions, using a first-principles method. Our calculations are conducted within the framework of the density functional theory, employing the full-potential augmented plane wave plus Gaussian orbitals method. We determine that both GdSn3 and CmSn3 adopt the AuCu3 structure type and exhibit ferromagnetic behavior in their ground states, with specific magnetic moments for Gd and Sn atoms. We find that CmSn3 displays a semi-conducting nature, whereas GdSn3 behaves as an itinerant ferromagnet with a defined Curie temperature. Our research reveals that all GdxCm1-xSn3 compounds exhibit ferromagnetism, but the Curie temperatures differ between the Gd-rich and Cm-rich phases. We observe that the Curie temperatures of these compounds are directly related to their compositions and exhibit either Gd or Cm-like magnetic moments depending on the range of x values.

The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the Standard Model, which incorporates a new fermion that interacts via quark-like gauge bosons, gluons, and electroweem weak bosons. This fermion acquires a mass in the TeV range through the Higgs mechanism, potentially giving rise to new matter and altering the universe's baryon-to-photon ratio. Various detection methods for these new particles and particles are explored across cosmic ray, astroparticle, and particle physics research fields. The model also predicts new mesons and baryons made of these fermions, such as quarkgluon plasma, gluonium, and other complex combinations. The electroweem weak symmetry breaking mechanism can result in the production of new heavy Higgs bosons, which the model allows for. Theoretical limitations of this extension are also discussed in the paper.

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Mann successfully demonstrated the uniqueness of the ordered generating sequences through his research. Moreover, he managed to extend this result to the infinite symmetric group and the alternating group A_n. Through this study, we further broaden this result to the finite complex reflection groups, specifically focusing on Type II and IV. Furthermore, we demonstrate the uniqueness of the ordered generating sequences for the special unitary reflection groups of Type II and IV, denoted as G(c) with $2 \leq c < \infty$, and the compact unitary reflection groups of Type II and IV, denoted as GU(c), with with $c > 1 + \sqrt{1+\frac{4}{s^2}}$.

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and an active galactic nucleus-based large-scale structure analysis, we've developed the spatial distribution and statistical properties of the intervening galaxy density along the path of SN Ia observations. Our study reveals that the average intergalactic matter density clumpiness around great clusters is approximately 1.6 times higher than in the surrounding void areas, with a corresponding lensing effect that results in a 0.04 magnitude increase in the brightness of the supernovae located within these clusters. Neglecting this effect in H0 measurements from Type Ia supernova observations could introduce a systematic error of up to 0.14 magnitude, potentially leading to inaccuracies in cosmological parameter estimation. By modeling the lensing effect, our research demonstrates its varying influence on the 220 NGRB bins, ultimately contributing to an overall bias in the Omega_b/h^3 estimation of around 0.00043.

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will rely significantly on solid-state devices that enable secure key distribution through photonic systems. A critical factor in achieving this goal is the creation of T centers in silicon, a material widely used in various applications due to its cost-effectiveness and versatility. Although the electronic structure of T centers in isotopically purified ^28Si has been theoretically explored, the definitive structure and position of these T centers remain undetermined experimentally. Through a series of sophisticated scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy techniques, we have successfully identified and characterized T centers in silicon, successfully distinguishing them from similar defects known as divacancies. By systematically varying the bias voltage and current in our experiments, we have gathered comprehensive data that can be correlated with theoretical predictions made for both T centers and divacancies, confirming our initial hypothesis.

For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is needed.
Different object detectors exploit scene context to enhance detection accuracy,
however, their effectiveness in our data set is untested as past studies past
randomized background for annotated objects. This study investigates two context-
aware object detectors – YOLOv3 and MASCAN – on a dataset of over 30,000 drawn
cats embedded into various cat-relevant and irrelevant background scenes.

The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$. Here, $\Omega$ is a bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^N$ that has a smooth boundary which touches the origin, $\varkernote\beta$ is non-negative, the function $f_i$ exhibits an indefinite sign, and it has an indefinite Kirchhoff growth behavior. The domain $\Omega$ is bounded in $\mathbb{R}^N$, the function $h_i$ is defined on the domain $\Omega$, and $m$ is given by a specific expression. By utilizing critical point theory and a change of dimension in a certain functional space, we can obtain a multitude of solutions for the system of equations under consideration.

We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors with a specific type of negative dependence known as Negatively Dependent on Coordinates (NDC). This exploration builds on a body of work that focuses on functions of functions that satisfy different forms of dependence relationships. Our work provides a distinct approach using a coupling technique directly applicable to NDC dependencies. The concentration inequalities we derive are specifically tailored to linear functions, quadratic forms, and another function type with an unspecified form, all of which satisfy the NDC dependency condition. Our development extends a result by Scott and Vu (2013) that dealt with quadratic forms through NDC dependencies and extends a product distribution result by Lutsko (2011) for quadratic forms through the same dependency framework. The techniques we employ also enable an extension of a product distribution result by Lutsko (2011) for linear functions, which generalizes a result by Lutsko (2010) that dealt with random matrices through NDC dependencies. The techniques we employ also serve to generalize a result by Lutsko (2010) that dealt with the number of cycles in a random graph G(n,p) through NDC dependencies in the subcritical and critical regimes.

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant properties. These properties initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and their associated coefficients, as well as elementary divisors – but also include additional data, such as coefficients from an quadratic residue field and forms of the Euclidean plane, categorized under GL_2.

A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques aim to increase the acceptance of incompatible kidney transplants. Yet, these methods carry elevated risks and costs, possibly displacing well-matched transplants from compatible donors and patients. This study develops a transparent analytical model of kidney desensitization, comparing its outcomes with those of natural kidney transplants and dialysis. Findings reveal that in high-incompatibility scenarios, patients undergoing desensitization transplants compete with others for low-quality kidneys, potentially reducing the need for dialysis but raising transplant risks and costs. Conversely, in low-incompatibility situations, the model suggests that accepting incompatible transplants may displace transplants from well-matched donors, thus offering no benefits over natural transplants. However, incorporating policy options like differential reimbursement for transplants can modify the model's results, providing valuable insights for health policy formulation.

This paper investigates whether the word2vec model genuinely comprehends the semantic meaning of the Loughran-McDonald financial polarity dataset, which spans over 40 years of corporate disclosures from the US energy sector. We first analyze the structural characteristics of these texts, focusing on their linguistic composition and the positional arrangement of words encoded as sequences of integers. Next, we apply standard natural language processing techniques typically used in human language analysis to the dataset. We then integrate neuroscience-inspired concepts and methodologies, including neural encoding, decoding, and the simulation of electrical brain signals, to further explore the internal relationships within the word2vec model's encoded sequences. Our findings reveal that the DM energy sector's dominant tone over time is reflected in the statistical asymmetry of its textual descriptions, which are predominantly numerically encoded as integers. We also discover that positively framed energy-related words tend to be associated with shorter, more compact words, which are positioned earlier in the text, while negatively framed energy-related words tend to be longer, more complex words, which are positioned later in the text.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instability with melting. The level-set technique's key advantage lies in its conservation properties and capacity to navigate highly intricate boundaries with ease. Furthermore, this approach can incorporate curved boundaries easily and without restriction, a significant benefit over other methods like front-tracking. Our numerical approach involves projecting the physical boundary onto a nearby level-set boundary, then restricting the solution to accurately represent the boundary's geometry. This has been demonstrated through various tests, encompassing 2D and 3D problems, as well as melting issues, showing the method's versatility and accuracy.

In multiagent learning settings, agents continuously learn from experience, gradually building knowledge about the game they're playing. Traditional analysis focuses on no-equilibrium learning algorithms, overlooking the fact that the learned learned strategies form a learned game. This article advocates for examining such algorithms in a rationalizability framework, proposing that a learned equilibrium is stable if it remains valid when the underlying game is analyzed through rationalizability. This concept is defined and key properties are established, providing a theoretical basis for understanding equilibrium stability in learned games.

An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions poses a more complex issue. Given the numerous components of modern PDF fits, including predictions from various processes such as fixed-order calculations, resummations, and the treatment of heavy quarks, manually matching formats is both time-consuming and prone to errors. In this context, a unified system consisting of JAX, PyPDF, and ROOT has been developed to streamline the entire PDF fitting process. This pipeline enables seamless integration of all relevant data, encompassing experimental measurements and theoretical predictions, to fit PDFs efficiently. It is demonstrated that the pipeline can replicate the well-known CT18 global fit by reproducing its key results, including PDF parameters, quark masses, strong interaction constant, parton threshold masses, and the matching and mixing coefficients for partons.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical analysis confirms the proposed method's higher sample efficiency compared to the conventional approach. Furthermore, the framework's versatility is demonstrated through successful applications to both policy optimization and probabilistic modeling with variational auto-encoders, outperforming the current method in terms of sample utilization.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous potential responses 
following any given conversation history. Our Study of Conversational Dialogue 
Directions, dubbed 'MultTalk', presents a challenging 10-way conversation tree, 
where each conversation turn involves a listener responding to a speaker who then 
switches roles. Our dataset encompasses 400 dialogue turns across 80 conversation 
threads with varying degrees of topic complexity. To address the diverse nature 
of our data, we trained a model to successfully predict conversation partners, 
trackers, and topic switches with high levels of accuracy. To our knowledge, 
MultTalk is the first conversious dialogue dataset to encompass a wide range of 
unpredictable conversation elements, pushing the boundaries of what is possible 
in the field of conversation analysis.

We present a methodology for creating rapid, comprehensive N-body simulation datasets for modified N gravitational theories by leveraging existing matter distribution data from general relativity. This approach involves calculating the deviations from lambda-CDM dynamics in modified gravity models on large scales, using N-body simulations of perturbations in a pre-existing matter distribution simulated with N-body methods. We specifically address the dynamics in conformal coupling frameworks, where modified N gravity effects are incorporated into simulations by adjusting the matter power spectrum and bias, solving a quadratic equation for the effective matter density. Our analysis, applied to f(R) gravity models, reveals significant variations in matter distribution simulations across different models and simulation datasets, ranging from minor adjustments of 5 to 10 percent in N-body halos to more substantial effects of 20 to 30 percent in clusters, with regional differences of up to 50 percent. This information is crucial for accurate interpretations of cosmological data in f(R) gravity models and other modified gravity theories.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, the collection of trajectories from these processes forms the tip set of the corresponding Gaussian free field.

MediaWiki, the underlying software for popular websites like Wikipedia,
supports a high-throughput, collaborative content creation environment that's
extremely user-friendly and feature-rich, yet its testing manual nature makes
it difficult to version control the entire page repository using control systems
like Git.
This project develops an extension for MediaWiki that integrates seamlessly
with Git, giving users the ability to easily version control their content while
retaining all of MediaWiki's collaborative advantages.
For our specific use case, our workingwiki package enables a highly collaborative
and version-controlled development environment for scientific projects.

This study investigates how turbulent jet flames respond to acoustic vibrations in a linearized model, with the goal of creating straightforward ways to predict stability in jet flames. To achieve this, we treated turbulent combustion as a source of flame acceleration and expressed it using linearized models. The analysis divided the closure model into two parts: one capturing the turbulent combustion's effect on mass flux using a stochastic approach, and the other modeling the interactions between mass flux fluctuations and acoustic vibrations using a radiation model. To evaluate these models in a linearized framework, we used existing empirical data from the literature and discovered that although the turbulent mass flux closure and radiation models have some variability, their average behaviors can be represented by simple, universal laws. These laws rely on key dimensionless numbers such as the Strouhal number, Mach number, and jet velocity. As a result, the response to vibrations becomes independent of specific conditions like jet diameter and ambient pressure. The existing models were then used to predict the response to vibrations in jet flames, and the predictions matched the available data very closely. The model also allowed us to identify the conditions under which these flames become unstable in theoretical conditions.

We investigate the neutrinoless double beta decay driven by an extremely light dark matter field interacting with neutrinos, particularly focusing on the decay parameter, which has a component that's heavily dependent on the field and can significantly enhance the standard neutrino contribution. Under the assumption that neutrinos are the source of neutrino mass, and given that the field's frequency is limited by observed cosmic structure, we derive constraints from the lack of cosmic production of electrons in $0
u eta eta$ decay. Additionally, we place new, unique constraints on the effective Majorana mass from the absence of excess electrons in searches for dark matter in bulk matter detectors, and we derive conditions under which experiments like XENONnT and LUX-ZEPPLIN II could potentially detect dark matter, provided their sensitivity to electron recoil is sufficiently high, and they are capable of detecting electron neutrinos involved in oscillations. Finally, we establish more stringent limits on the effective coupling between neutrinos and extremely light dark matter from current $0
u eta eta$ decay experiments, and we project that next-generation $0
u eta eta$ decay experiments will set the stage for potential discoveries of extremely light dark matter.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be applied to derive the nonlocal theory from a more fundamental level. By modifying the way the theory's field equations are derived, nonlocal gravity leads to a nonlocal constitutive relation, which plays a similar role in nonlocal electrodography as Maxwell's equations play a role in local electro-dynamics. This article is intended as a non-trivial mathematical framework for nonlocal gravity theory, extending the role of the fundamental tetrads to this context.

Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits has been hindered,
given the lack of information regarding the vast functional elements in the
genome. By integrating public expression data from 67 tissues and samples
with results from genome-wide association studies of 18 different human traits
through a method that leverages linked patterns in the genome, we have developed
a comprehensive model for tissue-specific trait influence. This model indicates
that many of the examined traits have significant associations across a wide
range of tissues, rather than being confined to a single tissue. In particular,
there is variation in the relevant tissues for the same trait across different
populations, and some traits have particularly strong associations with the
regional patterns in the genome in a wide range of tissues. By testing 6764
hypothetical statements taken from the studies, our model outperformed random
guessing and existing methods in locating the sources of associations accurately.
It also identified specific traits with strong associations with the immune
system's genes and the liver's gene expression patterns, and pointed to the
need to study the mechanisms underlying the association of height with the
brain's expression patterns. Additionally, we have developed a tool that makes
our model accessible for researchers to utilize in guiding further investigations
across 67 tissues.

This paper discusses recent findings from the LHC involving small systems studied
by the ALICE, ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Due to the growing significance
of QCD in small systems, particularly in situations with high multiplicity,
several studies with both proton-proton and electron-ion collisions are covered
in detail. Notably, the ALICE collaboration has discovered the suppression of
hadron composition in proton-proton encounters with high multiplicity, which is
highly similar to what's observed in the quark-gluon plasma. The ALICE
collaboration has also observed the quark-like suppression of hadrons at low
transverse momentum in electron-proton collisions, where a small quark-gluon
plasma tail within the hadron distribution is proposed as an explanation.
Additionally, the ALICE collaboration has investigated long-range correlations
arising from initial momentum anisotropy in low multiplicity events, finding
evidence for flow even in events with two jets. The ATLAS collaboration has
presented an in-depth analysis of two-jet events, finding evidence for jet
deflection that hints at collective behavior within small systems. The ATLAS
collaboration has also presented initial findings on two-jet event flow, finding
interesting similarities between small small systems and heavy ion collisions.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown growth in brightness over a short period suggest a specific type of astronomical object. The time it takes for neutron star binaries to return after becoming inactive is typically short, usually less than a year, based on the behavior of stars that do not explode supernova. However, V0614+295 and X zeta Per have long recurrence times, likely exceeding decades or even centuries. These extended time frames are uncommon for the objects within the Milky Way's center and point to V0614+295 and X zeta Per possibly not being located in the galaxy's center or not being located where neutron star binaries are expected to be found. In addition, the typical inactive X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center may not be low mass X-ray binaries as previously thought, but rather inactive neutron stars wandering through space.

THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystals, leading to the introduction of inertial influences on electrons. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, and the interplay of these forces with the spin-orbit and the redshift of energy levels. These effects can persist for a few picoseconds following the initial stimulation, and as they are neither thermal nor magnetic in origin, they respond uniquely to temperature and magnetic field variations. This niche application of electron-phonon inertia may prove valuable in identifying subtle intrinsic effects and advancing the field of quantum engineering.

Improving neural dialogue systems requires diverse conversations to mimic real human interactions. We introduce the Multi-turn Dialogue Natural Inference (MDNLI) dataset, which aims to measure the language generation diversity in multi-turn conversations. Consisting of over 780,000 three to five round conversations, MDNLI takes the MNI dataset as its foundation and includes a new annotation specifically for new information carried by the Natural Inference label. We propose the semantic diversity metric based on this label and assess the generation capacity of various models through multiple benchmark comparisons, including a series of multi-turn diversity guidelines. The examination reveals that incorporating content and style diversity prompts in single-turn dialogue can significantly increase the diversity of natural language, but also shows that current models struggle to generate diverse and in-depth conversations.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars is believed to be impacted by rotation, potentially allowing smaller objects to maintain this process. Objects that are capable of sustaining hydrogen fusion are thought to have minimal mass thresholds, with theory and observation indicating that a minimum mass for such objects could be as low as 0.005 solar masses due to factors such as age, composition, and, in the case of rotation, shedding limits.

To analyze the impact of rotation on object structure and determine the shedding limit, a new numerical model using the rotating object1D code has been developed. This code employs a semi-analytical approach to structure modeling and includes a novel, efficient method for calculating the shedding limit. The results obtained from this code have been compared with those from numerical simulations from the SPHINX project, showing that objects can tolerate a maximum rotation speed of approximately 0.5 to 0.7 times their critical value. The shedding limit leads to objects with a broad range of equilibrium states that can be parameterized by a dimensionless angular momentum. The density and temperature distributions in these objects are impacted by rotation, particularly in objects with higher angular momentum objects, which have a bulging shape, a density distribution concentrated at the equator, and a central temperature lower than in non-rotating objects. The model shows a range of objects that can exist, which extends beyond the established minimum mass for low-mass stars and short-lived objects with brief fuel supplies

The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is quite effective, 
allowing for detailed understanding of two-body decay processes. 
However, this analysis method is heavily influenced by accuracy and sensitivity 
to address non-ideal conditions of real detectors and theoretical assumptions, 
which must be addressed through the incorporation of  Monte Carlo simulations 
based on data-driven efficiency corrections and line shape corrections. 
Although these corrections are essential, they significantly increase the complexity 
and computational costs of amplitude analysis through the modification of likelihood 
functions. A current challenge is that modern analyses often exceed feasible 
computational limits due to the need to calculate corrections within simulators 
and re-fit the data with modified likelihood functions. 
In this study, we explore methods to streamline this process by expressing 
efficiency and line shape corrections as adjustments to the matrix elements 
within the formalism of amplitude analysis, thereby enabling direct incorporation 
into likelihood functions and improving computational efficiency. 
The applicability of this approach is specifically tested in the context of 
$B^0\to \eta\eta\eta$ decay analysis.

A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple contexts, including relativistic, non-relativistic phases and fireball radiations with radiative and adiabatic components.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number.

This paper investigates the potential of adding thrusters to the feet of bipedal robots to make their locomotion more efficient and adaptable. By adding thrusters, we aim to achieve three key objectives: achieving passive dynamic-like behavior in fully actuated robots, enabling the robots to recover from disturbances without relying on sophisticated control systems, and improving continuous gaits for heavy-load locomotion to enhance energy efficiency. To do this, we analyze the passive dynamics of passive robots and those with passive elements, and we also explore the application of thrust vectors to define a new type of invariant diagram that could facilitate passive dynamic-like behavior. This approach may provide a theoretical foundation for the successful integration of thruster-assisted locomotion in real-world applications, as demonstrated by an experimental setup with semi-passive ankle springs and thruster-assisted locomotion.

Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first observed in 1979 that over finite fields $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}$ from Laurent series to $k$ is expressible in a specific language, provided $t$ is included as a parameter. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series.

In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique for narrowing the effective CPU clock period without modifying the CPU's actual specifications. This novel method leverages the CPU's ability to slow down the execution of instructions by pushing software into a locked state, a capability that has not been utilized in previous attacks requiring memory access. This method is especially beneficial for memory-related attacks that cannot be executed in a fully automated manner, as it allows them to access memory in slowed timeframes, thereby accessing a broader range of attack vectors. This method was utilized to demonstrate an attack on the AES protocol and to develop a new, highly effective variant of the Flushtest in 2 MHz iterations. Furthermore, this method is applicable to other attacks that depend on memory access in extended timeframes, as evidenced by the development of a generic framework and the utilization of this method in the development of an attack on the Arx class of cryptographic algorithms, resulting in the creation of an entirely new variant of the Arx Flushtest. This method also enables Arx Flushtest to be made fully automated in MHz-range iterations.

A localized alteration in knot diagrams, called the (4,2)-Möbius switch, changes the crossing numbers of a link by at most 2 and its writhe by exactly 2. This algorithmic operation is distinct from other unknotting methods like the Whitney move, as it has no restriction on decreasing the crossing number for classical links and can arbitrarily increase the crossing number. Using the mod 2 Kauffman state polynomial, we've demonstrated that the (4,2)-Möbius move can also unknot all welded links. Interestingly, we found a specific welded knot type that cannot be unknotted through the (4,2)-Möbius move, but can be unknotted through the crossing change. Additionally, we explored the move's impact on various knot invariants.

We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles through integration produces a specific Vassiliev invariant, having a precise order of three. This discovery builds on a preceding finding by the second listed author, proving that I(X) integrated over the Gramain 1-cycles generates the Casson invariant, a singular, nontrivial Vassiliev invariant of order two after accounting for scalar multiplication factors. Similarities can also be drawn to a recent result by Polyak and Viro, who proved that combining the classical Jacobi torus link invariant with Gramain 1-cycles generates the Casson invariant.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options.

In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables multiple independent parties to train a unified model without exchanging data. The principles of vertical federated learning, where participants with disjoint variable sets collaborate, are examined in more depth. Given its advantages, various companies are now implementing this technology to jointly create machine learning models. However, we argue that without proper security measures, vertical federated learning protocols can expose sensitive information about an participant's private data. The attacks we have identified include: 1) inferring knowledge that is not apparent from the label of a dataset, such as the fact that it includes a person's phone number, and 2) reconstructing parts of an participant's private dataset. The latter can be achieved even when communication between the server and the participants is encrypted. Since this learning method allows participation by parties with large datasets, the impact of these attacks is particularly severe. To counter these threats, we argue that the current protocols must either be redesigned or implemented with additional privacy protections.

Kernel methods excel in performance but require substantial memory and computational resources, making them impractical for large datasets. In contrast, Random Fourier Features (RFR) offers a scalable alternative that maintains similar performance to kernel methods while reducing costs. However, RFR's efficiency relies on the variance of its estimates, which is determined by the feature mapping's range. This paper introduces a novel approach, DKNN, that replaces the traditional fixed range feature mapping with a data-dependent variant, significantly narrowing the feature mapping's range and enhancing RFR's efficiency. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that RFR using the new data-dependent PRR reaches the same accuracy as kernel NNE with significantly fewer knots, achieving speedups of 10x to 100x over kernel methods.

In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are effectively incorporated into the wreath products under their combined, or "product action," manner. To achieve this, we developed a distinctive approach known as the Cartesian Decomposition Method.

This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start by showing that if these hypersurfaces are compact and have non-negative M\"obius curvature, they must be pointings to parts of hyperspheres defined by their n-dimensional radius. Furthermore, in a specific case where the hypersurfaces are negatively M\"obius curved and compact, they are demonstrated to be properly embedded Clifto-Crighton hypersurfaces of a hypersphere defined by its (n-1)-dimensional radius and its subsequent radius of n+2 dimensions.

A new wireless networking concept called integrated information power signaling combines data transmission with an ambient frequency band, utilizing a near-field far-field distinction. In this setup, a special antenna array captures energy from the transmitted signals while another antenna receives data from the same signals transmitted by a base station. The goal is to determine the optimal resource allocation strategy that maximizes the total throughput of a network comprising multiple data flows and multiple devices, balancing throughput requirements and energy harvesting constraints. A primary optimization challenge arises due to the non-convex nature of transmitted signals, which is addressed by formulating approximations and applying matrix decomposition techniques to achieve a global solution. The research reveals that increasing the supply of energy can result in the elimination of RF power limits and the relaxation of minimum received signal strength requirements, leading to an ideal scenario where all devices are supplied with infinite energy and all transmission constraints are met. Furthermore, an inverse relationship is observed between the efficiency of energy harvesting and the elimination of RF power limits. Ultimately, the proposed resource allocation strategy aims to enhance the feasibility of intisw applications in future 5G and beyond networks.

Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating robust network systems. 
The examination of network avalanche dynamics has primarily been confined to binary 
node states. However, the real-world applications of this analysis are limited due 
to the fact that many systems involve significant amounts of damage at non-binary 
levels. This study aims to investigate avalanche dynamics involving level-proportional 
extraction levels and applies this analysis to Cayley tree networks. 
Our study shows that for a fixed perturbation level, the average avalanche size 
increases as the nodes' extraction level decreases. 
The relationship between avalanche size and extraction level conforms to a power law 
for large avalanche sizes, similar to what is observed in phase transition phenomena.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and the reflection of measurement signals. Overcoming these challenges is crucial for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers and determining the neutron star equation of state from gravitational wave data. A novel design called the sloshing Sagnac interferometer demonstrates increased sensitivity at high frequencies by reusing signal beams and exchanging signal and idler fields to reduce noise. This design's performance exceeds that of standard detector designs in specific frequency ranges, making it an promising candidate for improving the sensitivity of advanced gravitational wave detectors through modified optical systems.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems are being discussed, which MIMO randomness access without prior information involves base stations that cannot communicate with each other and are unaware of the positions of other MIMO-based base stations within their coverage areas. In this setup, some MIMO-based base stations are found unable to detect some of the nearby base stations due to the allocation of random time-frequency resources in this protocol. In order to address this issue, these protocol-related problems are mapped to an agent-based model, which can provide a solution to communication protocol problems in large-scale MIMO systems by overcoming limitations in scalability. These solutions can be applied to real-world data regarding MIMO-based base station distributions in urban environments, which reveal that protocol-related issues result in only a small fraction of based stations experiencing them, specifically around 2% to 10%, and that scaling the system to larger numbers does not significantly exacerbate this problem.

Recent observations of young stellar objects have revealed a surprising presence of
filamentary structures in the dust emissions of their surrounding disks.
Theoretical models have struggled to replicate this feature, particularly in the
outer regions of these disks. We have developed a new instability arising from
vertical shear that can generate structures in the disk without requiring a dense
gas/dust interface or spiral arms. Investigating the extent to which this
instability can produce structures similar to those observed, we used the
Radiative/Non-radiative version of radiative transfer codes. These simulations
demonstrated sufficient structures to be detectable in observations, particularly
in the low frequency range of millimeter and sub-millimeter wavelengths.
Filamentary structures were produced in both simulations with and without
radiative effects, but the simulation with radiative effects also exhibited
structure in higher frequency range of millimeter wavelengths. The R11 version of
radiative transfer code struggled to accurately model the simulations with a
dense gas/dust interface, but the RAYCODE version successfully modeled them.
This code comparison serves as a useful benchmark for evaluating the accuracy
of radiative transfer codes in high-resolution simulations. Ultimately, this study
has shown that vertical shear instability can generate structures in the dust
emissions of young stellar object disks.

A novel scalar vector interaction, called BigApple force, based on the spontaneous
breaking of chiral symmetry and the subsequent creation of a sigma meson
condensate, is introduced in this study. This force, resembling the Paris force,
is incorporated into finite nuclei through the Relativistic Mean Field model, and
its effects are compared with those of the sigma meson, demonstrating clearer
patterns in in-matter nucleon antinucleus ratios and reducing discrepancies in
nuclear equation of state saturation properties. Furthermore, applications to
neutron stars, including predictions for mass-radius relationships, are explored.
