This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series, as well as real-world applications in neuroimaging and oceanography. Furthermore, an open-source R package is made available to facilitate the use of MFSSA in practice.

The power law decay $P(\xi_n(a) \leq \max(\xi_n(a + ),\xi_n(a -)) \geq x_n$ for Local times of stochastic processes is an indicator of temporal-reversal invariance and has been established for Brownian motion. This study focuses on the number of steps $S$ in a one-dimensional simple symmetric random walk where the local time at the origin falls below its typical maximum value, demonstrating that this duration follows the same decay pattern and persists across all states. Additionally, we provide simulation evidence of its universal nature, develop scaling functions for the walk's first return and its conditioned version, and leverage these insights to enhance the Vaserstein-Meier algorithm's efficiency by an order of magnitude in certain tests.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with 3000 Watts of unconfined plasma provides helical radio frequency plasma for 210 MHz to 370 MHz frequencies. Until now, this plasma source has been operating in lower harmonic modes, but it is designed to be capable of switching to a higher, more realistic mode found in helical plasma sources. To do this, the source must be designed to match the helical match box, and a study of the source must be done to identify its characteristics and ultimately confirm the helical mode. A previous study of the source was done using Langmuir probes, but they failed to fully capture the plasma source features, in particular the plasma features perpendicular to the magnetic field lines, the plasma rotation, and the plasma structure along the field lines. A new diagnostic system, consisting of retarding field analyzers, rotating electron energy analyzers, and mass spectrometers, has been successfully installed and has yielded detailed information on the plasma characteristics, including profiles along the magnetic field lines and, in some configurations, rotation and evidence of the helicon mode of the source.

Identifying biological nuclei in tissue images is a critical task in pathology, yet it poses a significant challenge due to the variability in nuclei appearance. A notable issue with existing deep learning-based segmentation methods is the tendency to directly replicate image noise as boundaries of biological nuclei. To address this problem, a researcher developed a novel approach that combines a point cloud deep learning algorithm with a unique convolutional network for nucleus segmentation. This enhanced network is capable of reconstructing nuclei in areas previously missed by the initial detection stage. Evaluations of this approach in three distinct tissue images demonstrate the network's performance surpassing current state-of-the-art methods in terms of nucleus detection accuracy.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G with the same central character and gamma factors, under the condition that r is even and they share the same supercuspidal constituents, it can be inferred that the two representations are isomorphic. However, if r is odd and the representations have a trivial central character, the same conclusion holds true and they are also isomorphic.

Deep Neural Networks have gained popularity due to their success in various applications, but their underlying mechanisms have been difficult to explain, particularly in the context of graph-structured data where GCN models are commonly used. To address this issue, our research delves into the internal workings of GCN models by developing a compareable lightweight sub-model that mirrors their complex computations. Through this approach, we demonstrate that GCN models are difficult to interpret as they combine feature normalization and linear transformations to propagate information within the graph. However, our findings also reveal an interesting connection between GCN models and matched filtering techniques, which is supported by theoretical evidence. This discovery has significant implications for GCN models, enabling us to fine-tune their bias settings to optimize their performance. We validate these insights empirically by conducting extensive experiments that show the prescribed BIAS settings can be used as an effective diagnostic tool for GCN models, as well as a means to enhance their performance when applied as a preprocessing step before more advanced models.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity coupled to a scalar field can be derived from a Chern-Simons action for a SO(2,1)xU(1) gauge group under specific conditions. Solving the equations of motion for this system yields two distinct equations that resemble the equations for conformal field theories with left and right central charges. By exploring possible transformations of the Chern-Simons gauge group, we can describe static and rotating soliton solutions and rotating hairy black holes. Additionally, the solutions found in this f(R) theory of gravity with a "square root" R are found to be fully equivalent to those found in general relativity.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, enhances the estimation of medical conditions such as cancer by visualizing and measuring tissue stiffness. Non-linear convolution-based methods, in particular, provide precise images of stiffness but can mislead in assessing how far tissues have moved laterally. This issue is especially pronounced near image boundaries due to distorted point-spread functions in these methods. Although various strategies have been proposed to mitigate this problem, existing solutions fail to deliver an effective solution. This research introduces a novel approach known as Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA), which mimics a favorable axial response similar to linear imaging and minimizes lateral movement estimation errors. Experimental evaluations on both simulated and actual ultrasound elastography data demonstrate that VSSA achieves a 4.5 times improvement in axial resolution and offers superior performance in assessing lateral movement when compared to the traditional time-gating method.

Algorithms and correctness proofs are both essential for ensuring that computational systems function properly. However, securing both can be a challenging task. To address this, we introduce an effective method that links an algorithm's desired behavior with its expected correctness properties. This approach enables developers to create software more efficiently and with greater reliability, by leveraging the power of Coq for verifying desired properties. As a result,Coq can automatically check the desired properties of the algorithm, ensuring its correctness.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately the same order as that required by the best possible algorithm, but with the advantage of a polynomial runtime.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies.

Due to the limited parton content of muons, especially at low $x$, the potential of high-energy muon colliders to achieve unprecedented energy scales can be significantly constrained. To mitigate this limitation and reach higher energy regimes where hadron colliders might be within reach, we propose using TVS-based muon colliders with energy scales exceeding 100 TeV. In this context, the W and Z part of the muon PDF becomes non-negligible, particularly for processes involving two electroweak bosons. We demonstrate that the "W and Z part" of the process can account for up to 50% of the total cross section at $\sqrt{s}=100$ TeV and $50$ TeV for two EW boson scattering. Furthermore, we contend that the WB approximation fails to provide an adequate description of the process. As a result, a revised approach, the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, integrating both the WB approximation and the muon PDF, is necessary to provide an accurate calculation of process cross sections.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is most evident in model-free methods, model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning offers additional advantages due to its shared learning
of a dynamics model and rewards. However, it is not clear how tasks that have
different subgoals, models, and rewards are best handled in this context. We
investigate this issue using a comprehensive framework and a large set of
synthetic and real-world robotic control experiments. We find that task
swapping, a common practice of sharing networks for the state value and next
state prediction, frequently results in performance deterioration. Moreover,
it is often worse than performing each task separately. Our studies also reveal
that sharing a single network leads to catastrophic interference between tasks.
In response, we propose a simple and effective solution of using multiple
modular networks for each task that prevents catastrophic interference. We
provide code for our experiments at this repository: https://github.com/
aleksandrzabowski/Modular-Shared-MLP-MB-MTRL-SBXL-. Our results suggest that
using separate modular networks is beneficial when dealing with a wide range of
different tasks in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

In solving inverse problems, we aim to recover an undisplayed variable from given data. This task is inherently ambiguous, resulting in multiple plausible solutions. Traditional methods produce a single best-fit solution, whereas recovering the solution's probability distribution offers valuable insights into possible solutions. Current distribution estimation techniques, such as GANs, can be unreliable due to their uncommitted nature. In our study, we develop a regularized canonical conditional GAN post-inference to characterize the solution space's solutions more effectively. By applying constraints, we enhance the accuracy and quality of recovered images in problems like computed tomography and deblurring, as demonstrated in our experiments.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective, focusing on a specific fractionally pinned state. However, we notably discover that both invariant center manifolds and stable manifolds do not exist in fractional order systems. This finding is a significant implication of our research.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens, as their positions and physical properties are tracked over time. One such screen, responsible for the scintillation of pulsar B1133+16, is located 2.2 kpc away, with an uncertain position. By examining the change in the pulsar's trajectory relative to the sky and taking into account the distribution of electrons around the galaxy, we were able to determine that this screen is in our galactic neighborhood. It has an electron density of 0.018 cm^-3 and is situated 43' from the galactic center, in the second quadrant. This finding adds to the limited knowledge of the structure of the galaxy's local interstellar medium, particularly within our spiral arm.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to predict audio signals using just three pieces of information: the transcript, the speaker's gender, and their fundamental frequency (F0). Building on WaveNet, QPNet adapts dilated convolution layers to enhance efficiency and accuracy. It employs dynamic skip connections and separate dilated networks for pre- and post-voicing samples, capturing the non-stationary nature of speech. By utilizing distinct networks and different dilation rates for each sample type, QPNet captures the unique characteristics of speech waveforms. The results show that QQPNet generates high-quality speech with low mean squared error and strong naturalness, perceived in subjective evaluations.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. This connection facilitates the establishment of the interest of working with shadows of bicategories, which in turn facilitates the development of a natural modification of THH that remains invariant under certain conditions and leads to the proof of the invariance of the R-fraction of the K-theory of a category under double categorification.

Our primary goal in this project is to pinpoint the source of visually present sounds in videos with a single camera through deep learning, addressing sound source localization in a challenging scenario where the camera's viewpoint, distance, and angle relative to the sound source's emission point are taken into consideration. To achieve this, we develop a comprehensive, multi-view dataset, which is the first of its kind categorized by point-of-view conditions, consisting of 45,000 seconds of video across nine different settings. Our approach involves training a single camera model using a vast number of features extracted from the visual content, resulting in a method that achieves an F1 score of 0.89 in an unbiased evaluation across all datasets. Furthermore, our results indicate our model's ability to generalize across new point-of-view conditions, whereas baseline methods fail to do so effectively.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks have utilized a variety of metrics, including Euclidean, Riemannian, and Lorentzian metrics. However, there is no unified approach that specifically addresses the advantages of using a Lorentzian metric in the context of GCNs. Our research reveals that a Lorentzian metric can offer beneficial implications for various applications, such as when the graph data resides within a high-dimensional space that must be efficiently stored, or in scenarios where the network is training on an inherently nonlinear and constrained manifold. To harness these benefits, we developed a novel LN-GCN model that leverages a Lorentzian metric for computing graph aggregations. Our initial evaluations of this model were conducted on manifold learning, with plans to expand its applications to other domains in the near future.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of a wave equation and an acoustic Laplace equation coupled together. The source term in this model represents a characteristic property of the structural component, specifically its density. The source term (observational data) for this problem is the middle field of this coupled PDE model, while the displacement field and pressure field at given points serve as boundary conditions at both the beginning and end of a specific time period. The problem was first introduced in the work of Iadecia and Leugering in 2017, where they sought to identify a second physical parameter in addition to density. Our work, however, aims to prove the uniqueness of this density parameter based on previous studies that established sources for the problem.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, providing
a statistical basis for the Tsallis assumption. We also suggest that the Tsallis
assumption holds, along with exploratory analyses suggesting possible biological
implications.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, only one of the possible harmonic gauges avoids giving rise to ghost modes in the perturbation's mass term.  The principle of minimal modification is then applied to construct a non-linear version of the harmonic gravity model, which is shown to satisfy the harmonic gravity model's necessary conditions.  Furthermore, initial steps towards developing a path integral formulation for the non-linear harmonic gravity model and applying it to compute the model's partition function and physical observables are begun.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using their Weyl-Wigner representations also known as Pumbria functions. 

This reveals that these states are closely related to a type of thermal equilibrium classical statistical systems that exhibit equilibrium between a Fermi-Dirac or Bose-Einstein distribution of temperatures and a classical harmonic environment with the same temperature.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillations that arises only when a specific singlet scalar is included. This particular model achieves the necessary conditions to prevent the Higgs potential from becoming unstable and ensures neutrino oscillations and dark matter behavior meet observable requirements, all within the relatively narrow range of the new gauge coupling constant from 0.3 to 0.5. We determine the minimum and maximum values of the new mediator mass at approximately 2.4 TeV and 6 TeV, respectively, and identify the required parameters of the dark sector that can be verified through future experiments.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, specifically within a paramagnetic regime. Through our study, we investigate the magnetic characteristics that emerge from this mixing, utilizing both Green's function Cumulant expansion and numerical Green's function analysis to quantify these features. Our findings demonstrate that for metals with a single electron, the $t_{2g}$ majority-spin band is the most deeply bound, whereas for metals with one hole, the $e_g$ minority-spin band is the least bound. These results are in direct agreement with recent experimental findings from X-ray absorption spectroscopy in iridium-based oxides, where the researchers observed a mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals that cannot be fully explained by the broadening of the inner-shell momentum.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. A significant finding is that, for toric blow-ups, the relative I-functions remain invariant, while for the blow-ups along torus-fixed subvarieties, they are related through a transformation called the Gamma conjecture. A key result of the study is the ability to apply these findings to prove both the half of Gamma conjecture proposed by Clader, Long, and Looijenga, as well as the full version proposed by the same team. Additionally, they are used to establish equivalence between the relative I-functions for the compact Crepello-Morrison toric blow-up and the original I-function, thereby validating the quantum mirror theorem for this particular type of intersection. Furthermore, the study provides a more comprehensive understanding of the Gamma operation's impact on I-functions for toric blow-ups. A set of explicit formulas has been derived to describe this effect.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, yet its underlying fundamentals remain unclear. This study employs counterfactual analysis from decision theory to investigate the fundamentals of generative adversarial-based methods for medical imaging, focusing on facilitating model interpretability and enhancing diagnostic accuracy. The proposed approach utilizes a carefully constructed convolutional neural network baseline to test if the generative adversarial networks' capacity for model interpretability exceeds traditional methods. The results obtained through this line of research and code are made available publicly. The findings reveal that although the imagines produced by the model are effective at differentiating between disease categories, the model's simplicity causes it to excel at classifying diseases that are over-represented in the training data, highlighting the need for more sophisticated architectures and loss functions. The study's limitations and future research directions are also discussed.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling various file formats commonly used
in machine learning and other types of classification, including CSV, ARFF, and
SQL. The tool is designed to manage large datasets with numerous variables and
millions of records. It offers a wide range of visualization techniques, such as
scatter plots, box plots, histograms, heat maps, and various types of principal
component analysis visualizations. ViDaExpert also includes sophisticated analysis
functions like missing value detection, data type conversion, statistical
summarization, outlier identification, and engineered variable creation. The
application is user-friendly and customizable, allowing users to create new
visualizations and analysis methods through plug-ins.
